newsitem.title: USA: Advanced Micro Devices reports loss for the quarter.
newsitem.headline: Advanced Micro Devices reports loss for the quarter.

text.p: Semiconductor maker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Monday reported a $38.4 million loss for the third quarter as the company strove to compete with Intel Corp.'s popular Pentium chips.

The loss of $38.4 million, or 28 cents a share, including a one-time charge of $6 million taken to cover severance pay for laid off workers and compared with a profit in the year-ago period of $42 million, or 30 cents a share.
Sales in this year's quarter were $456.8 million, down sharply from $606.9 million in last year's third quarter.
The beleagured semiconductor maker has been trying to compete in the microprocessor market against Intel, which dominates the field with its Pentium processors.

AMD last year was making money selling 486 microprocessors -- the generation of personal computer chips that preceeded the Pentiumn -- to makers of less expensive PCs. But the market for 486 microprocessors dried up this year as Intel made cheaper and cheaper Pentiums available.
AMD also sells flash memory chips and other specialised chips such as programmable logic chips.

The Sunnyvale, Calif.-based company has invested millions in developing microprocessors and building big chip factories to manufacture them. Those costs were partly to blame in the loss, AMD's chief executive said.
Revenues from the AMD unit that makes microprocessors grew from the second quarter, with its Pentium-alternative "K5" chip doubling in shipments to 500,000, said Chairman W.J. Sanders III.
But Sanders added "revenues are currently insufficient to absorb the substantial fixed costs of maintaining our strategic commitment to the Microsoft Windows-compatible microprocessor market."
AMD's 28-cents-a-share loss was not as bad as Wall Street had expected. Analysts on average expected AMD to lose 36 cents a share, according to a tally by First Call.
Still, Bear Stearns analyst Nimal Vallipuram said the smaller loss is no reason to get excited about the stock.

"Results are marginally better because of better capacity utilization," Vallipuram said. "But AMD still hasn't addressed the most important issue. They do not have an Intel compatible microprocessor at the same performance as mainstream Pentiums."
AMD developed the K5 product in response to the Pentium. But currently available versions of the K5 are comparable to entry level Pentiums, he said.

Monday in a separate statement, AMD announced two new versions of its K5 chip -- the AMD-K5-PR133 which is a 133-megahertz chip and the AMD-K5-PR120, a 120 megahertz chip. But mainstream Pentiums are now 166 megahertz or 200 megahertz, Vallipuram pointed out.
